one_liner: Experimental Ruby gem that compiles type-annotated Ruby methods to Crystal, then Wasm; about 11-14x CRuby on recursive fib(40).
what_it_does: A class does `extend Cry::Wasm`, puts a Crystal type signature (`cry [:Int32], :Int32`) before a method and calls `cry_build`; the gem re-parses the method's source with Ripper and Sorcerer, adds Crystal type restrictions, compiles the result with `crystal build --target wasm32-wasi` and wasm-ld, loads it into Wasmer (wasmer-ruby) or Wasmtime (wasmtime-rb), and redefines the Ruby method to call the Wasm export. Arguments and returns are limited to integer and float scalars, integer/float arrays (copied through Wasm linear memory) and Strings; default, keyword and block arguments, instance variables and Symbols are not supported.
how_it_is_fast: The speedup is ahead-of-time static typing: once the method is Crystal code with fixed-width Int32 arguments, the recursion compiles (through LLVM to Wasm, then the Wasm runtime's compiler to machine code) into direct calls with machine-integer arithmetic, removing CRuby's method dispatch and its tagged-Integer arithmetic with overflow-to-Bignum checks. There is no algorithmic change; the gem only translates the same Ruby source.
when_to_use: Experiments with a small, self-contained numeric Ruby method (integer or float scalars in, scalar out) that is called once and runs for a long time, like the fib(40) benchmark, where the single Ruby-to-Wasm crossing is negligible.
When you want a sandboxable Wasm artifact of a Ruby hot loop and already have Crystal, wasm-ld and the wasm32-wasi libs on macOS or Linux.
Prototyping how much static typing alone buys over CRuby before writing a C, Rust or Crystal native extension.
when_not_to_use: Methods that return arrays or take large arrays: every element is copied through Wasm memory, the Wasmer adapter reads it byte by byte in Ruby, and the README warns this can be slower than pure Ruby.

Code that relies on Ruby Integer semantics: the Int32 signature makes arithmetic fixed-width, so the benchmark's own fib definition overflows Int32 at fib(47) where CRuby would return a Bignum; overflow behaviour inside Wasm is not documented.

Production use: version 0.0.0, labelled experimental, not published on RubyGems, Windows unsupported, CI badge failing as of 2026-10-12, and it needs wasmer-ruby and wasmtime-rb from git master (wasmer-ruby's last commit is from October 2023 and its README lists Ruby 2.6-3.0).
Short, frequently called methods: both runtimes are slower on the first call (README plot at n = 1), and each call goes through a Ruby-level wrapper that builds argument arrays.
Comparisons against a modern CRuby: the baseline Ruby version and whether YJIT was on are not stated, so the 10x figure may shrink with a JIT-enabled CRuby (not measured).

integration.dependencies: Crystal compiler, wasm-ld (LLVM lld), wasm32-wasi libs from lbguilherme/wasm-libs (rake vendor:wasi_libs), sorcerer gem, wasmer-ruby and/or wasmtime-rb from git master (Rust toolchain to build them)
integration.min_toolchain: Ruby >= 2.7 (gemspec); CI uses Ruby 3.2 with the latest Crystal from crystal-lang.org/install.sh; no Crystal version pinned
integration.platforms: macOS and Ubuntu (CI); Windows not supported
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each class holds one Wasm instance and store shared by all its objects
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the Ruby method body is reused unchanged, but the class must extend Cry::Wasm, every compiled method needs a `cry` signature and a `cry_build` call, and only Crystal-compatible code with the supported argument types can be compiled

gotchas: Benchmark harness: the Wasm module is a Crystal -O0 build, because Compiler#set_options stores :release but build_command never adds --release (Crystal's default is -O0; --release means -O3 --single-module), so the 11.5x and 13.9x come from unoptimised Crystal output that only the Wasm runtime's own compiler optimises. fib_bench.rb makes one fib(40) call per report, so it measures recursion inside Wasm, not the Ruby-to-Wasm call path, and the README names no CPU, Ruby, Crystal, wasmtime-rb or wasmer-ruby version. Both arms run the same recursion and fib(40) = 102,334,155 fits in Int32, so no correctness bug sits behind the numbers.

Bug in lib/cry/compiler.rb: `if (options.output = '/dev/stdout')` is an assignment, not a comparison, so passing an output path to cry_build (wasm_out) makes build_wasm return the compiler's empty stdout instead of reading the written file; only the default stdout path works.
Every array or String argument is copied into a fresh Pointer.malloc buffer in Wasm memory on each call and never released (the wrapper ends with '# FIXME: Release memory').

The WASI sandbox is opened wide: the Wasmtime adapter passes the full host ENV and ARGV and inherits stdout/stderr; the Wasmer adapter maps the host current directory using test-program boilerplate ('wasi_test_program', '--test'); and each `Klass.new` re-runs the module's `_start` on the class's shared instance.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only when the host program is Ruby: the other wasm-language siblings (Speedy.js, wasm-perf, AutoZig, msf/wasmplay's Zig build) compile to Wasm for JavaScript or WASI hosts and beat V8 JavaScript or Emscripten C++, while cry-wasm is the one entry that accelerates CRuby methods, at a much lower maturity level than those.
verified_claims_summary: The README's Benchmark.bmbm output from December 2022 (examples/fib_bench.rb, no CPU, Ruby, Crystal or runtime versions given) shows one fib(40) call taking 5.31 s user time in CRuby, against 0.462 s for the same method compiled to Crystal Int32 code and Wasm under wasmtime-rb and 0.381 s under wasmer-ruby, about 11.5x and 13.9x (derived from page data). The Wasm module was built at Crystal's default -O0, and the claim that Wasm is about twice as slow as native Crystal is the author's unpublished measurement.
status_note: Experimental and effectively dormant: feature work ended in December 2022 (last code commit 'Use to_unsafe to create a pointer', 2022-12-26), later commits through 2026-06-19 are Renovate CI bumps, the CI badge reads failing, and the gem is version 0.0.0 and not on RubyGems; MIT-licensed and small enough to read in an afternoon.
